question: How guitars make sound
title_suggestion: How Guitars Make Sound? What Science Actually Says

sources.title: 17.5 Sources of Musical Sound
notes: Instrument timbre depends on the relative mix and intensity of fundamentals and overtones.
Resonant sounding boxes couple string motion to surrounding air.

sources.title: 16.3 Wave Speed on a Stretched String
notes: Wave speed on a stretched string follows v = square root of tension divided by linear mass density.
Frequency depends on wave speed and vibrating length.

sources.title: Strings, standing waves and harmonics
sources.publisher: University of New South Wales, Music Acoustics
notes: A plucked string supports standing-wave modes; high-frequency components fade faster after the pluck.
Harmonics and plucking point influence the spectrum.

sources.title: 44.21 — Guitar
sources.publisher: University of California, Santa Barbara, Physics Lecture Demonstrations
notes: Fretting changes vibrating length and pitch; tuning pegs change tension.
Plucking near the bridge emphasizes upper harmonics.

sources.title: Guitar Pickup
sources.publisher: National High Magnetic Field Laboratory, Florida State University
notes: Steel-string motion changes a pickup's magnetic field and induces an electrical signal.
The signal goes to an amplifier and loudspeaker, turning electrical energy back into sound.

sources.title: The strings and the soundboard
sources.publisher: KTH Royal Institute of Technology / Klaus Wogram
notes: The bridge transfers string vibrations to the soundboard, whose resonances shape radiated sound.
Excitation position and soundboard resonances affect radiation.

editorial_angles: The string sets pitch, but the instrument must couple mechanical energy into surrounding air.
Pitch is governed by vibrating length, tension and mass per unit length.
Timbre emerges from harmonics, attack, decay and resonances.
Acoustic guitars radiate sound through a moving soundboard; electric pickups convert string motion into a signal.
The hollow body is not merely a volume knob; it participates in a coupled mechanical-acoustic system.
